query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: Using machine-learning trained interatomic potentials for high-entropy alloy liquid-phase simulations paired with free-energy perturbation analysis can accurately and efficiently determine melting temperature, enthalpy of fusion, entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and other liquid-phase thermodynamic properties, matching traditional thermodynamic integration within acceptable error margins while notably reducing computational cost.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloys modeled initially with standard empirical liquid-phase EAM potentials.
generation.intervention: Replace the conventional EAM potentials with ML-trained interatomic potentials and substitute thermodynamic integration with a free-energy perturbation method in the liquid-phase simulation.
generation.conditions: Simulations performed at melting conditions for a range of high-entropy alloy compositions where high-quality training data for ML potential is available.
generation.structural_mediator: The ML potential refines the free-energy landscape representation, mediating improved accuracy in computed structural and thermodynamic properties across the melting transition.
generation.mechanism: The ML-trained potential better captures complex atomic interactions in the disordered liquid state, and free-energy perturbation directly computes the thermodynamic derivatives, thus allowing more efficient and accurate determination of phase transition properties compared to traditional integration methods.
generation.predicted_outcome: The ML and free-energy perturbation approach will yield melting properties that agree with those from traditional thermodynamic integration within an approximate 5–10% error margin and will reduce computational time by an estimated 30–50%.
generation.baseline: Traditional simulations employing empirical EAM potentials and thermodynamic integration.
generation.boundary: The approach is expected to be valid for high-entropy alloy compositions where the ML potential has been adequately trained; its performance beyond these compositions or under extreme conditions remains uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative performance improvements (error margins and efficiency gains) depend on the quality and range of the ML training data, with possible deviations if the ML potential does not capture the necessary liquid-phase physics accurately.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct parallel simulations on a representative set of high-entropy alloys using both the ML-based free-energy perturbation method and the traditional thermodynamic integration approach. Evaluate the melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and additional liquid-phase thermodynamic properties, along with the computational time required for each approach.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ML-based approach produces property predictions that differ by more than 10% from those obtained via traditional thermodynamic integration or fails to achieve a computational efficiency improvement of at least 30%, the hypothesis is falsified.
